general: The Shire is a place where the greatest concerns are the quality of the harvest and the proximity of second breakfast.
Green hills roll away in every direction, dotted with the round doors of hobbit-holes that smell of wood smoke and fresh bread.
There is nowhere in Middle-earth quite as comfortable as a well-appointed hobbit-hole with a good fire and a stocked larder.
The folk of Hobbiton minded their own business admirably, which made the arrival of wizards something of an event.
Six meals a day is not greed in the Shire; it is simply the recognition that living well requires a serious commitment to eating.
The Party Tree had seen many a celebration, but none quite so elaborate or so bewildering as the one with the firework dragon.
Pipe-weed, old books, and a comfortable chair by the fire — some hobbits required nothing more from life and were perhaps the wisest.
Bag End sat above the Hill like a crown, its round green door polished and its garden always in impeccable order.
The water mill turned slowly in the afternoon sun, and the smell of the River Brandywine drifted up through the meadows.
A hobbit's idea of adventure was discovering that the bakery had a new variety of seed-cake, which was quite adventurous enough.
In the Shire nobody hurried, everybody gossiped, and the most controversial question was whether Old Toby or Longbottom Leaf made for finer smoking.
The road from the Shire to anywhere worth going was long and dangerous, which was precisely why most hobbits never took it.
Bilbo Baggins was considered eccentric primarily because he had left and come back, which was not something respectable hobbits did.
The smell of a hobbit-hole — of pipe smoke and mushroom soup and damp earth and old leather — is a smell that has no equivalent anywhere else in the world.
frodo: I used to stand at my door and watch the road, wondering where it went; now I know, and the knowing changes the watching.
The Shire is still beautiful when I return to it; I just see it from a different angle now, one that includes a great deal of darkness.
There are days when I miss it so much it feels like a wound — the small certainty of it, the smell of the earth after rain.
Some things you can only fully love after you have lost them, or come close to losing them, which is its own kind of grief.
sam: I always said I wanted to see elves, Mr. Frodo, but I never imagined I'd have to go quite this far or through quite this much to do it.
The Gaffer's garden is the finest in Hobbiton, and when this is all over I plan to make mine even finer, which will cause him considerable annoyance.
A good tater and a bit of salt — that's what I'd give half of Middle-earth for right now, if I'm being honest about it.
Home is worth fighting for, and so is a friend, and if you've got both to fight for then you've got no cause for despair.
gandalf: The Shire is one of the places in this world that gives me reason to believe the light is worth preserving.
I have smoked Old Toby at hobbit doors from one end of the Shire to the other and never found a better excuse to linger.
Do not underestimate the Shire; the courage that was bred into hobbits here has saved this world more than once.
There is something in the Shire that even Mordor cannot reproduce or corrupt — a fundamental contentment, a refusal to be impressed by darkness.
gimli: I will admit, grudgingly, that these Shire-folk have an enviable relationship with food that even a dwarf must respect.
Give me stone and deep places over green hills, but I can see why a creature of simple tastes would choose to live here.
The hobbit-hole architecture is more sophisticated than it first appears; whoever designed them understood the thermal properties of earthworks.
